title: When someone sneezes
hookLine: the one who sneezes says alhamdulillah, and the hearer says, may Allah have mercy on you (Bukhari)
tomorrow: an essay asks what you're really searching for. where do you start?

cards: The tickle. The eyes squeezing shut. The breath that hitches once, twice, and then: achoo.
A sneeze is the one thing your body does that nobody can do politely. It happens on buses, in meetings, in hospital rooms, in the middle of a sentence. And often, somebody says something back.
Is there a right thing to say? In this path there is, and it isn't one line. It's a small conversation in three turns, kept in al-Bukhari, built around the body's least dignified noise.

teach.b: Turn one belongs to the person who sneezed: alhamdulillah, praise be to God.
Turn two belongs to whoever hears it: yarhamuk Allah, may God have mercy on you.

Turn three goes back to the sneezer, who answers with a blessing of their own: yahdikumullah wa yuslih balakum, may God guide you and set your affairs right. Three people's worth of kindness, from one sneeze.
Al-Bukhari also keeps a small scene that explains the order. Two men sneeze near the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He answers one and not the other.
The second asks why. Because, the Prophet says, he praised God and you didn't.
The mercy follows the praise. So a sneeze becomes a tiny lesson in noticing: something ordinary just happened to the body, and the first word is thanks.
Not thanks for the sneeze, exactly: thanks that the body works, that the breath came back, that you are still here to be a little embarrassed.
In the same collection there's a line people tend to find surprising: God loves the sneeze and dislikes the yawn.
One clears the head; the other, the hadith says, comes from carelessness. English speakers have their own reply, bless you. This one simply keeps going, until both people have blessed each other.

how: When a Muslim sneezes they say alhamdulillah; anyone who hears replies yarhamuk Allah, and the sneezer answers yahdikumullah wa yuslih balakum, following hadith in al-Bukhari.

o: a prayer said to ward off sickness after a sneeze
a polite apology said by the one who sneezed
a three-turn exchange of praise, mercy and blessing

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.

s: the hearer speaks first after a sneeze
the sneezer goes first, with alhamdulillah. the mercy follows the praise.
a hadith in al-Bukhari says God loves the sneeze and dislikes the yawn
a surprising line from the same collection.
the exchange ends once the hearer says yarhamuk Allah

games.q: in class, the kid next to you sneezes three times and says nothing. you know the three turns. what fits them best?
o: say yarhamuk Allah anyway, loudly, so they learn the rule.
nothing's owed yet; the mercy follows the praise. a quiet bless you is still kind.
remind them they forgot to say alhamdulillah.
games.why: in al-Bukhari the Prophet answered the man who praised God and not the one who didn't. no lecture, no correction: the reply follows the praise.

practice: Say the whole exchange out loud, slowly, and feel each phrase in your mouth: alhamdulillah. Yarhamuk Allah. Yahdikumullah wa yuslih balakum.
Then rest, and let your breath come and go on its own, the same breath a sneeze interrupts.

wordCard.voice: When someone sneezes. Praise from the sneezer, mercy from the hearer, guidance in return: a three-turn kindness from al-Bukhari.

orig.note: Arabic: yarhamuk Allah, may God have mercy on you. The hearer's turn after a sneeze.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: mercy on you, said back to a stranger's sneeze. That completes fourteen daily remembrances.
